title: The final salok: air, water, earth
hook: pavan guru paanee pitaa maataa dharat mahat: air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother; day and night the nurses (Japji, salok)

segments.voice: Yesterday, sabad, and your line: the word is minted. Were you patient once, on purpose? That was the last pauri. Today, the short verse that closes the whole Japji. Day two hundred thirty.

Think about the first few minutes of your life. Before you had a name, before you knew anyone's face, three things met you. Air rushed into your lungs, and you cried. Water: you'd been floating in it for months, and someone washed you in it. And then you were laid down, held, on something solid. Air, water, ground. They were there before any teacher, any parent's voice, any word. Every morning since, they've been there again, without being asked. After thirty-eight stanzas of climbing, the Japji doesn't end at the top of the ladder. It ends with one short verse, and it comes all the way back down to these three.
screen: `YOUR FIRST MINUTES.` → `AIR, WATER, GROUND.` → `THE JAPJI COMES BACK DOWN.`

segments.voice: The Japji opened with a short verse, a salok, before the first pauri: aad sach, true in the beginning. And it closes with one more. Here's how it begins: pavan guroo paanee pitaa maataa dharat mahat. Air is the Guru, water the father, and earth the great mother. Air as Guru is worth a moment. The breath is what carries every word, every hymn, every sound of the Name. Without air, no teaching reaches anyone. Then: divas raat due daaee daaiaa, khelai sagal jagat. Day and night are the two nurses, a woman and a man who care for a child, and in their lap the whole world plays. It's a family picture of creation: parents, nurses, and all of us, children, playing. Then the tone turns serious. Good and bad deeds are read out in the presence of Dharam, the righteous judge. By their own actions, some come near, some stay far. And the last lines: those who remembered the Name have finished their hard work and gone. Nanak says, their faces shine, and many others are set free along with them. So the Japji ends on shining faces, and not alone: others go free with them. Many Sikhs today quote pavan guroo paanee pitaa when they speak about caring for the earth. If the air is your teacher and the earth your mother, you don't treat them like trash. And notice where it leaves you. Not in a far realm, but right here, breathing, drinking, standing on the ground.
screen: `PAVAN GUROO — AIR IS THE GURU.` · `WATER THE FATHER, EARTH THE MOTHER.` · `DAY AND NIGHT, THE TWO NURSES.` · `FACES SHINE, AND OTHERS GO FREE.` · then, large: `AIR, WATER, EARTH.`

segments.voice: If you can, open a window or step outside. If not, stay where you are. Breathe in slowly and feel the air come in: that's the Guru, in the salok's picture. Take a sip of water if you have some, and feel it go down. Then press your feet into the floor, into the earth beneath the building. Air, water, earth. Stay with the breath now, in and out, letting the three hold you, the way they did in your first minutes. The bell holds the time.
Pavan, air, the breath that carries every word. The short verse that closes the Japji: air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother, day and night the nurses, and faces that shine.
Your line: air, water, earth. Today, step outside once and breathe, and treat one of the three a little more kindly than usual. Day two hundred thirty.

screen: `DAY 230 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: CAMP 4 CLOSE: THE WHOLE JAPJI.`

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib every morning, ending with this closing salok, and its first line is often quoted by Sikhs speaking about care for the environment.

original.note: Gurmukhi, Japji closing salok: air the Guru, water the father.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nature poem tacked on the end.
what it means: creation as a family that raises us, a reckoning of deeds, and faces that shine with many freed alongside.
what a scholar hears: a close version of this salok appears later in the Granth credited to Guru Angad; daaee and daaiaa are a female and a male nurse.
